Improving scalability of multi-agent deep reinforcement  learning with suboptimal human knowledge
Dingbang Liu1,2 · Fenghui Ren1 · Jun Yan1 · Guoxin Su1 · Wen Gu2 · Shohei Kato2
Auton Agent Multi-Agent Syst (2026) 40:2 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10458-025-09729-1
Abstract Due to its exceptional learning ability, multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL)  has garnered widespread research interest. However, since the learning is data-driven and  involves sampling from millions of steps, training a large number of agents is inherently  challenging and inefficient. Inspired by the human learning process, we aim to transfer  knowledge from humans to avoid starting from scratch. Given the growing emphasis on  the Human-on-the-Loop concept, this study focuses on addressing the challenges of large- population learning by incorporating suboptimal human knowledge into the cooperative  multi-agent environment. To leverage human experience, we integrate human knowledge  into the training process of MADRL, representing it in natural language rather than spe­ cific action-state pairs. Compared to previous works, we further consider the attributes  of transferred knowledge to assess its impact on algorithm scalability. Additionally, we  examine several features of knowledge mapping to effectively convert human knowledge  to the action space where agent learning occurs. In reaction to the disparity in knowledge  construction between humans and agents, our approach allows agents to decide freely  which portions of the state space to leverage human knowledge. From the challenging  domains of the StarCraft Multi-agent Challenge, our method successfully alleviates the  scalability issue in MADRL. Furthermore, we find that, despite individual-type knowledge  significantly accelerating the training process, cooperative-type knowledge is more desir­ able for addressing a large agent population. We hope this study provides valuable insights  into applying and mapping human knowledge, ultimately enhancing the interpretability of  agent behavior.

1  Introduction
Empowered by deep learning, multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL) has tran­ scended the limitations of historical tabular methods and found application in complex sce­ narios, stimulating widespread research interest [8, 13, 32, 52]. As a rapidly evolving field,  MADRL has achieved rapid development with numerous frameworks proposed. These  approaches leverage novel technologies in communication [14, 47], attention mechanisms  [20, 33], and graph theory [25, 43] to address the challenges of non-stationarity and partial  observability [32]. Nevertheless, scalability remains a critical attribute of MADRL, as it  facilitates autonomous collective learning behaviors among agents. In many engineering  and scientific disciplines, algorithms require sufficient scalability to ensure effective coop­ eration [4, 17, 27]. However, training a large number of agents presents inherent difficulties.  The joint action-state space expands exponentially with the number of agents, leading to the  curse of dimensionality [5, 28]. Compounded by sparse rewards and sample inefficiency  [3, 7], agents encounter “start-up” challenges [45] and frequently stagnate in local optima,  rendering learning impossible in the worst-case scenarios. While effective in small groups,  many state-of-the-art algorithms still struggle to scale to a large number of agents [13, 46].
To mitigate the burden of exploration and overcome the curse of dimensionality, knowl­ edge transfer methods have attracted significant research interest in the context of large- scale multi-agent systems [6, 39]. Inspired by human learning processes, these methods  enable agents to adjust their strategies based on prior experience, thereby avoiding the need  to learn from scratch when facing unfamiliar scenarios. As the most intuitive and prevalent  source, transferring prior knowledge from human trainers has received considerable atten­ tion [12, 54]. In 2017, Nahavandi [30] further highlighted the significance of the Human- on-the-Loop concept. In this paradigm, while agents execute tasks autonomously, humans  act as monitors or supervisors to facilitate more intelligent decision-making. Following this  trajectory, an increasing number of studies have investigated integrating human knowledge  into the training process to guide agent learning [19, 24, 54]. A prominent line of research  focuses on extracting prior knowledge from expert trajectories via imitation learning [40,  48] to address sequential decision-making problems. Although an increasing number of researchers have investigated the feasibility of  transferring knowledge from humans, the utilization of human knowledge in large-scale  multi-agent systems necessitates further exploration. Currently, human knowledge is pre­ dominantly applied in single-agent tasks [22, 29], whereas its implementation in multi- agent systems has not been fully discussed. Despite impressive achievements in DRL, most  single-agent methods are not directly applicable to multi-agent scenarios, as applying them  in an unprincipled manner can precipitate catastrophic negative transfer [6]. While some  existing works address the multi-agent setting, the scope is often restricted to a small num­ ber of agents [2, 49]. Furthermore, human knowledge is typically applied indiscriminately,  and the methodology for mapping knowledge from humans to agents remains in its nascent  stages [12]. However, knowledge in multi-agent systems encompasses various types and  attributes, with different types of knowledge potentially having varying impacts on agent  learning. Additionally, the scalability effects can differ depending on the number of agents

involved. Nevertheless, incorporating human knowledge holds potential to mitigate the  scalability challenges inherent in large-scale systems, as numerous studies have demon­ strated the efficacy of integrating human knowledge into RL agent learning.
Motivated by these challenges, we attempt to integrate different types of human knowl­ edge into the action space to address the scalability issue in large-scale cooperative multi- agent systems. Representing human knowledge in natural language, we explore the effects  of different types of human knowledge on varying numbers of agents. As agents develop  policies within the action space, we also consider several features of knowledge mapping to  better map human knowledge onto the action level. Empirical results from challenging sce­ narios in the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) [36] demonstrate that: i) leveraging  human knowledge enables our framework to mitigate scalability issues in MADRL. Further­ more, the framework is capable of automatically filtering out improper knowledge during  the learning process to prevent negative knowledge transfer; ii) individual-type knowledge  significantly accelerates the training process, whereas cooperative-type knowledge exhibits  greater efficacy as the number of agents increases; and iii) regarding the mapping of coop­ erative-type knowledge, constraints are necessary, and the subset of participating agents  should be limited to ensure better scalability. Conversely, individual-type knowledge per­ mits broader application across large agent populations. We hope this work provides general  guidance on human knowledge transfer and enhances the interpretability of agent behaviors.
In the following sections, we will first discuss the related work on knowledge transfer in  Section 2. Then, the background is introduced in Section 3. Subsequently, our approach to  applying human knowledge is elaborated upon in Section 4. The experimental settings and  results are presented in Section 5. Finally, the conclusion and future work are discussed in  Section 6.
2  Related work
Even state-of-the-art MADRL algorithms face challenges in addressing the substantial sam­ ple complexity inherent in large-scale agent systems. Given the high computational cost  associated with exploration, knowledge transfer has emerged as an indispensable strategy  for enhancing the scalability of MADRL. Predicated on similarities in data, tasks, or models,  knowledge transfer leverages previously acquired information from comparable domains,  thereby diminishing the reliance on extensive data samples. One primary implementation  within MADRL involves repurposing solutions derived from agents in prior tasks. Alterna­ tively, numerous studies advocate for the utilization of knowledge from auxiliary sources,  notably human expert demonstrations [6].
2.1  Knowledge transfer among agents
Motivated by the concept that agents can benefit from the knowledge of peers, various  knowledge reuse methods have been proposed to simplify the learning process.

To enhance learning efficiency, parameter sharing is proposed, where knowledge is trans­ ferred among agents through the shared parameters [15]. By sharing a centralized policy  network among agents, Shao et al. [38] achieved scalability over 40 agents. However, the  application of parameter sharing typically necessitates agent homogeneity [56]. Further­ more, several studies have emphasized the critical importance of diverse policy genera­ tion in scenarios involving large agent populations. Conversely, parameter sharing tends to  enforce high policy similarity, thereby hindering the capacity of the algorithm to manage  large-scale populations effectively [3, 50].
Beyond knowledge sharing during training, agents can also derive learning from prior  tasks. Transfer learning reuses knowledge acquired in distinct tasks requiring similar skills  to address complex agent interactions [44]. Since this approach requires discerning the cor­ relation between tasks, the issue of negative transfer remains a persistent challenge [26].  Similar to transfer learning, curriculum learning aims to improve agent capabilities gradu­ ally through a designed curriculum. By progressing from small-scale scenarios to those with  many agents, this method can compensate for specific deficiencies and positively impact  long-term development [28, 31]. Nevertheless, the curriculum at each stage is typically  selected manually by human experts. Furthermore, the fixed neural network structure limits  knowledge completeness, as the number of agents varies between curricula [45].
However, a primary limitation of the aforementioned knowledge transfer methods is that  the extracted knowledge is abstract and lacks interpretability. As the neural network oper­ ates as an end-to-end “black box”, knowledge is implicitly stored within the parameters.  Consequently, evaluating the efficacy and quality of the transferred knowledge proves chal­ lenging. Transferred parameters are occasionally ill-suited, potentially leading agents to  reuse unrelated knowledge. Compounding this issue, a general metric to address this evalu­ ation problem remains absent [6, 18, 39].
2.2  Knowledge transfer from human
As the “black box” approach is unsuitable for critical applications, the transfer method  should be interpretable, prompting an increasing number of researchers concerning the  Human-on-the-Loop idea [12]. Intuitively, transferring knowledge from human trainers is  straightforward and profitable. Based on human policy itself, the most common source,  various frameworks have been explored to effectively harness human knowledge. By per­ sonally executing tasks, human trainers transmit their policies to agents [37]. Agents then  record human demonstrations in the form of action-state pairs, allowing them to mimic  demonstrated policies based on imitation learning [19, 23], inverse reinforcement learning  [41, 55], and other human-focused methods [6, 29]. By mitigating the challenges posed  by sample complexity and sparse rewards, these methods improve training effectiveness,  obtaining extensive discussion.
While mainstream research primarily relies on step-by-step action demonstrations, sev­ eral studies have sought to reduce the requisite human effort. To mitigate sample ineffi­ ciency, Le et al. [22] combined imitation learning with reinforcement learning. Duan et  al. [9] further reduced the computational burden associated with rule-based and imitation  learning. Additionally, Zhang et al. Nevertheless, the effective utilization of human prior knowledge proves significantly  more challenging within MADRL. Due to non-stationarity and the existence of multiple  Nash equilibria, most single-agent methods are unsuitable for multi-agent scenarios. To  adapt to multi-agent systems, Yang et al. Research closely  aligned with our approach includes that of Han et al. [16], who proposed leveraging agent  exploration capabilities to mitigate negative transfer. However, their work did not investi­ gate the scalability issue or examine how prior knowledge influences the training process  across varying agent population sizes.
Based on prior literature, addressing the scalability issue via human knowledge remains  underexplored. Human knowledge is typically transferred to a limited number of agents,  as designing complex rules or reward systems for large-scale systems is laborious. Conse­ quently, the appropriate harnessing of human knowledge for large agent populations neces­ sitates further investigation. Furthermore, as machines become increasingly integrated into  daily life, it is imperative that agents accurately adhere to human instructions. Neverthe­ less, research on translating human natural language into machine language for RL agents  remains in its infancy [12]. In contrast to previous works, we propose representing knowl­ edge in human language, positing that this approach holds the potential to resolve scalability  issues. Rather than applying human knowledge indiscriminately, we further consider the  type of knowledge and the method for appropriately mapping the knowledge into the action  space for RL agents.

3.2  Scalability with knowledge transfer
Due to the high exploration costs inherent in large-scale action-state spaces, transferring  prior knowledge from related tasks has demonstrated effectiveness in scenarios involving  an increasing number of agents [13, 45]. Given that human knowledge represents the most  intuitive and accessible resource, human-guided approaches, including imitation learning  [19] and inverse reinforcement learning [41], have been adopted to mitigate learning dif­ ficulties through human demonstrations. Furthermore, Yang et al. [48] applied human inter­ vention to improve cooperation within drone swarms. However, these methods often heavily  rely on high-quality expert demonstrations, which can be laborious to collect, especially in  challenging tasks. This motivates us to explore leveraging suboptimal human knowledge to  facilitate the learning process of agents while preserving their autonomous learning capa­ bilities, thus enhancing scalability.
4  Methods
In this section, we describe our method, which combines human knowledge with the  MADRL algorithm to provide general guidance on knowledge utilization and simplify the  required human effort. First, we formalize each type of human knowledge and illustrate the  process of mapping abstract human knowledge into the action space. This enables agents to  autonomously decide on the portions of the state space where knowledge should be reused  to mitigate the impact of inappropriate knowledge. Second, we show the exploration within  the extended action space and the entire training process.
4.1  Human knowledge representation
Humans excel at abstracting complex action sequences into simple explanations. In con­ trast to demonstrations coupled with specific states, we formulate human knowledge as  natural language explanations that describe things to perform or avoid without providing  specific actionable instructions. In the following experiments, we use SMAC as our testbed to assess the impact of dif­ ferent human knowledge types on addressing the scalability issue in MADRL. In addition to win rates,  we analyze the usage rates of each knowledge type and specific knowledge within each type  to identify general patterns in knowledge application and mapping. All experimental results  are based on five separate runs with distinct random seeds.

5.4  Results
Applying human knowledge mitigates the learning difficulties of agents and improves the  scalability of MADRL. Even when pure MADRL algorithms struggle with a large num­ ber of agents (as seen with 35 agents in Fig. 3), all types of human knowledge effectively  address initial learning challenges. Notably, each piece of transferred knowledge within  each human knowledge set covers only a small portion of the action-state space. Addition­ ally, the human knowledge set may contain inappropriate advice, such as “always escape”  (underlined in Table 1). Despite based on such low performance human prior knowledge,  benefited from the proposed knowledge exploration process and MADRL learning updates,  all types of human knowledge consistently outperform pure MADRL algorithms across  various numbers of agents Fig. 3.
Still, different types of human knowledge exert varying influences on the learning process.  On the one hand, individual-type knowledge, which can be applied more indiscriminately,  significantly accelerates training and proves beneficial in the early stages for overcoming  the “start-up” problem. On the other hand, cooperative-type knowledge is more desirable  for mediating coordination problems in large agent populations. Moreover, to achieve more  scalable knowledge mapping, it is more appropriate to define knowledge as cooperation  within a small agent group with upper limits.

Although knowledge with mapping functions that control large  agent groups exhibits high using rates when only a few agents are present, its utilization  rapidly decreases as more agents become involved. Conversely, knowledge with mapping  functions associated with small agent groups displays lower utilization but greater stabil­ ity. For cooperative-type knowledge, to enhance its knowledge scalability, it is preferable  to design mapping functions that involve small agent groups. Through the integration of human knowledge, our approach effectively handles scenarios  involving a large number of agents, which would otherwise be challenging and impractical to  learn from scratch. We hope that this work can offer insights into addressing the learning difficul­ ties inherent in systems with large agent populations and further improve the interpretability of  agent policies, taking a step toward multi-agent systems that cooperate effectively with humans.
Nevertheless, several potential extensions exist for future work. In this study, human  knowledge is represented using hard rules, which may require a certain level of domain exper­ tise and limit flexibility. Additionally, since the proposed method primarily follows a rein­ forcement learning process, extra effort is needed to explore the effective use of the provided  knowledge, thereby increasing the requirement for knowledge quality. Given that represent­ ing human knowledge with minimal human effort has attracted increasing research attention  [54], future studies may explore the use of high-level human feedback to address scalability  issues in MADRL. Meanwhile, quantifying the relationship between knowledge quality and  scalability thresholds also represents an intriguing direction. Furthermore, as a growing num­ ber of studies focus on heterogeneous agents [11, 42], applying human knowledge within  heterogeneous agent systems presents another promising avenue for future research.
